title: Using the diffraction-grating equation
prior_knowledge_summary: Lesson 9 established unit-safe wavelength calculations and proportional reasoning for double-slit fringes.
Lesson 8 established that coherent waves superpose constructively when their path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.
Lesson 6 established diffraction as wave spreading at a gap.
new_learning: Use d sin θ = nλ for diffraction-grating maxima.
Convert a grating ruling density into slit spacing d.
Interpret order number, symmetric maxima and the largest possible order.
not_yet_taught: describe the use of a diffraction grating to determine the wavelength of light

blocks.title: How can one beam make many bright directions?
content: A laser shines normally on a grating with hundreds of narrow lines in each millimetre. A central bright spot appears, then matching bright spots on both sides. Why are only particular directions bright?
A grating does not send light into just one pair of fringes. Its many equally spaced openings make sharply selected directions where the emerging waves reinforce.

figure.purpose: Create the need for order number and symmetric grating maxima.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch of a normally incident laser, a grating, a central maximum and three matching maxima on each side. Label only centre, first, second and third order, with sparse coloured rays and no equation.
figure.alt_text: A diffraction grating produces a central maximum and matching orders on both sides.

blocks.title: The path condition becomes the grating equation

definition.displayed_content: the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase

content: This is the formula to remember for a diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ. Here d is the separation of adjacent grating slits in metres, θ is the angle from the straight-through central direction, n is the order number 0, 1, 2, ... and λ is wavelength in metres.

At a maximum, waves from adjacent slits travel paths that differ by n wavelengths. They arrive in phase and reinforce. At zero order, n = 0 and θ = 0°. At first order the path difference is λ; at second order it is 2λ.

figure.purpose: Connect the geometry d sin θ to a whole-wavelength path difference.
figure.brief: Rectangular enlarged teacher sketch of two adjacent grating slits separated by d, parallel emerging rays at angle θ from the normal, and a right-triangle projection labelled d sin θ. Beside it show nλ as the required path difference.
figure.alt_text: The path difference between rays from adjacent grating slits is d sin theta.

blocks.title: Convert lines per millimetre before using the equation
content: A grating marked 500 lines mm⁻¹ has 500 equal spacings in 1 mm. Its spacing is d = 1/(500 mm⁻¹) = 0.00200 mm = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ m.

For λ = 600 nm in second order, sin θ = nλ/d = 2(600 × 10⁻⁹)/(2.00 × 10⁻⁶) = 0.600, so θ = 36.9°. An independent check is physical: sin θ is between 0 and 1, and second order must lie farther from the centre than first order.
It feels natural to use 500 as d because that number is printed on the grating. It fails because 500 lines mm⁻¹ is a density, while d is one separation. Take the reciprocal and convert the unit.

figure.purpose: Make reciprocal spacing conversion and unit conversion a visible sequence.
figure.brief: Rectangular four-step worked layout: 500 lines in 1 mm, d=1/500 mm, d=0.00200 mm, d=2.00×10^-6 m, followed by a compact second-order substitution. Highlight reciprocal and powers of ten in different colours.
figure.alt_text: A ruling density is converted to slit spacing before the grating equation is used.

blocks.title: Orders are symmetric, but θ is measured from the centre
content: For normal incidence, the same positive angle and negative angle satisfy the condition. The first-order spots are at +θ₁ and -θ₁, the second-order spots at +θ₂ and -θ₂. The angle between a matching pair is therefore 2θ, not θ.
If a diagram gives 74° between the two third-order maxima, use θ = 37° in d sin θ = nλ. If it gives 37° from the central direction to one maximum, use 37° directly.
The central maximum is order zero, not a pair. Orders 1, 2 and 3 each give two maxima, one on either side.

figure.purpose: Prevent confusion between one-sided angle θ and the angle between symmetric maxima.
figure.brief: Rectangular comparison panel. Left: central normal to +third order labelled θ. Right: -third to +third labelled 2θ. Use the same rays and colour coding in both panels.
figure.alt_text: The angle between symmetric maxima is twice the angle from the central direction to one maximum.

blocks.title: Find the largest order that can exist
content: Because |sin θ| cannot exceed 1, nλ/d must be at most 1. Therefore n ≤ d/λ, and the largest possible order is the greatest whole number not exceeding d/λ.
For d = 2.50 × 10⁻⁶ m and λ = 580 nm, d/λ = (2.50 × 10⁻⁶)/(580 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.31. Orders 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 can exist; order 5 cannot because it would require sin θ = 1.16.

The value 4.31 is not an order. Order counts complete whole-wavelength path differences, so use the integer below it. A check with the equation gives sin θ₄ = 0.928, which is allowed, while sin θ₅ exceeds 1.

figure.purpose: Show possible-order reasoning as a physical sine limit rather than a rounding rule.
figure.brief: Rectangular order ladder from n=0 to n=5. Mark n=0 to 4 as possible, n=5 crossed out, and place a side scale showing sin theta up to the boundary 1. Include 4.31 between orders 4 and 5.
figure.alt_text: The sine limit allows orders up to four but rules out order five.

blocks.title: A reliable grating route
content: First identify whether the grating value is a spacing or a line density. Convert to d in metres. Next identify n and decide whether the stated angle is θ or 2θ. Then rearrange d sin θ = nλ, substitute, and check that |sin θ| ≤ 1.

Use symmetry to interpret pairs of maxima, and use n ≤ d/λ to test possible orders. This lesson uses given grating and light data. Planning measurements and determining an unknown wavelength experimentally belong to Lesson 11.

figure.purpose: Consolidate the calculation decisions while preserving the Lesson 11 boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular flow chart: density or spacing, convert d, choose order n, inspect angle θ or 2θ, rearrange, substitute, sine-limit check. Add a final closed box labelled experimental procedure in Lesson 11 without showing steps.
figure.alt_text: A decision flow checks spacing, order, angle and physical possibility before reserving experimental procedure for the next lesson.

visual_rules.style: colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch on rectangular white paper

misconceptions_addressed: The printed lines-per-millimetre value is the slit spacing.
The angle between symmetric maxima is θ.
A non-integer value of d/λ should be rounded to the nearest order.
Every positive integer order must exist.
